channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Rail
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] Renfe passenger data was taken through compromised Adif servers; Adif says no rail-operations system was touched
item.category: Top Story
item.description: Adif, Spain’s state railway infrastructure manager, detected unusual activity late on 24 September, took its websites offline as a precaution and restored them on 26 September. On 25 September the train operator Renfe said passenger data, mainly names and email addresses, had been obtained from Adif servers compromised earlier; it reported no impact on banking or financial data and has given no passenger count. Adif says no system related to railway operations was affected and trains ran normally. A 500 GB haul and AI-assisted tooling, aired in Spanish media and in Shieldworkz’s 30 September analysis, remain unconfirmed by either company, and no actor has been named. This is an IT and customer-data incident, not an OT one. It leads because it is still the only confirmed intrusion at a national rail operator in the 30-day window, and it came through a partner link both sides trusted by design. - Renfe and Adif statements as reported by Europa Press (via Alicante Plaza) and AFP (via The Local); Shieldworkz analysis as reported by Industrial Cyber; the 500 GB, AI-tooling and attribution points are unconfirmed; the partner-link framing is our editorial assessment - Adif detection 24 Sep 2026; Renfe statement 25 Sep 2026; Adif websites restored 26 Sep 2026; Shieldworkz analysis 30 Sep 2026; no newer official statement found as of 16 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] The FBI and Secret Service say FortiBleed credential theft against FortiGate firewalls is still running — across every critical-infrastructure sector, with no CVE to patch
item.category: Incident — Active credential-theft campaign against boundary firewalls, agency-confirmed, all critical-infrastructure sectors
item.description: The FBI and the US Secret Service issued a joint advisory on Tuesday 6 October warning that the FortiBleed campaign against internet-facing Fortinet FortiGate firewalls and SSL VPN gateways remains an active threat. It is not a software vulnerability and has no CVE: per the agencies, it exploits reused or leaked credentials and legacy SHA-256 password storage. Researchers describe credential stuffing and spraying from leak dumps and infostealer logs, offline cracking of extracted password hashes on a GPU cluster, and a Go-based sniffer that passively captures authentication traffic across 24 protocols. Some owners were locked out after the attackers created their own administrator accounts and deleted or reset the legitimate ones. The agencies say compromised firewalls have served as ransomware entry points, and the FBI advisory links the access to Payload ransomware. Cybersecurity Dive reports that targets span all 16 US critical-infrastructure sectors — a list that by definition includes transportation systems — naming energy, communications, and food and agriculture among them. The most-cited scale figure, more than 86,644 working device credentials across 194 countries, is SOCRadar’s count as of 19 June, not a new tally; SOCRadar says it has confirmed at least 12 ransomware deployments stemming from the access and describes the operator as a Russian-speaking access broker, which is a researcher assessment, not agency attribution. No OT system compromise and no rail victim has been described. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: FortiGate is one of the most common firewalls at the IT/OT boundary of railroads and transit agencies, and a stolen administrator credential there is a way to rewrite segmentation without exploiting anything. - FBI and US Secret Service joint advisory JCSA-20261006-01 (IC3); reported by The Hacker News and Cybersecurity Dive; scale and actor profile per SOCRadar; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Advisory issued 6 Oct 2026; reported 7 Oct 2026; scale figure as of 19 Jun 2026

item.title: [High] Attackers took over web-managed refrigeration controllers at about 700 French supermarkets — a food-sector attack, and a direct lesson for contractor-managed station and depot plant
item.category: Incident — Food & retail sector OT attack in France; carried here as a cross-sector lesson, not a rail incident
item.description: From the night of 11–12 October, attackers remotely took control of internet-reachable refrigeration management controllers in French supermarkets and forced them into continuous or extended defrost, with setpoints of up to about 50 °C, spoiling stock; the Paris prosecutor reports outbreaks of fire at some sites. A second wave on the night of 12–13 October hit stores with Dixell controllers. Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on 13 October that about 700 of France’s roughly 10,000 supermarkets were affected, and Carrefour, Coopérative U, E.Leclerc, Intermarché/Netto and Monoprix have confirmed impact. CERT-FR’s alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 named Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers on 12 October, added Copeland and Dixell xweb on 13 October, and in its 16 October update says attack campaigns are probably still ongoing. Danfoss and Copeland say most affected units are older, end-of-life models. No group has claimed the attack, no ransom has been demanded and the entry route has not been established; the national cyber agency ANSSI has mobilised, and the Paris prosecutor’s cybercrime section has opened an inquiry. Reports of targeting in other European countries come from one security firm, Sekoia, and have not been confirmed by any foreign authority. Separately, Claroty’s Team82 showed on 13 October that an AI coding agent, steered by a researcher, reproduced a previously disclosed Danfoss exploit chain to root in about 28 minutes; it does not say those flaws were used in France. This is not a rail incident and it does not count toward this page’s threat level. It is here as our editorial lesson: stations, depots and tunnels run the same kind of contractor-supported, web-managed plant — HVAC, ventilation, pumping, lighting — and this attack needed little more than reachability and outdated controllers. - CERT-FR alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 (version 3, 16 Oct 2026); AP via News4JAX for the Finance Minister’s figure; SecurityWeek for retailer, vendor, Sekoia and Le Monde details; Claroty Team82 research; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Attacks on the nights of 11–13 Oct 2026; CERT-FR alert 12 Oct, updated 13 and 16 Oct 2026; Team82 research 13 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] US authorities seize the scanning and phishing tools of a China-based contractor whose named targets included airports in Japan and Poland and a US power company
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Nation-state-linked tooling disrupted; transportation hubs among named targets
item.description: The Justice Department and FBI announced on 8 October court-authorised seizures, in the Western District of Pennsylvania, of domains behind two tools: Microscan, a Python web application carrying more than 1,300 penetration-testing scripts, and FishHub, a spear-phishing and malware-delivery service. US authorities tie both to Integrity Technology Group, a China-based company sanctioned last year. CyberScoop describes the tools as Flax Typhoon-linked, while Cybersecurity Dive says the activity mimics that group and others such as Ethereal Panda rather than equating them. A Mirai-variant IoT botnet supported Microscan, and a joint FBI, CISA and NSA advisory notes persistence through VPN software. Court documents name Microscan targets including a South Carolina power company, airports in Japan and Poland, gas and power companies in Taiwan and a multinational NGO, with Taiwanese universities hit by FishHub phishing; no target’s compromise is confirmed. CISA’s Chris Butera said Chinese government-affiliated actors continue to position themselves within critical-infrastructure networks, including operational technology systems. No rail operator is named. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: transportation hubs are on the target list, and pre-positioning of this kind typically starts with exactly what Microscan automated — scanning internet-facing services for known flaws. - DOJ and FBI seizure announcement and joint FBI, CISA and NSA advisory, as reported by CyberScoop and Cybersecurity Dive; target list from court documents per Cybersecurity Dive; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Seizures announced 8 Oct 2026; reported 8–9 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Mandiant says ShinyHunters is back exploiting Oracle PeopleSoft by encoding one letter past WAF rules — transportation is among the sectors with compromised systems
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Mass exploitation of an enterprise application, transportation among sectors hit
item.description: Google Threat Intelligence and Mandiant reported on 25 September a renewed mass-exploitation campaign by UNC6240, the group known as ShinyHunters, against CVE-2026-35273, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in the PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub (the /PSEMHUB/ path), rated CVSS v3.1 9.8. The flaw was first exploited as a zero-day against academic institutions in late May and early June, and Oracle has had a fix out since June. The new wave requests /%50SEMHUB/ instead: WAF rules that match the literal path miss it, and WebLogic decodes and routes the request anyway, reaching, in Mandiant’s words, “systems whose operators may have believed their WAF rules had mitigated the exposure”. Mandiant counts “dozens of systems” compromised globally across higher education, technology and IT services, healthcare, agriculture, transportation and government, names no victims, and says it has notified more than 100 organisations whose addresses matched vulnerable endpoints. The tooling includes JSP web shells, Neo-reGeorg tunnels, a SIDEEYE backdoor delivered in a trojanised Light Alloy media-player installer, and MeshAgent. CISA has listed CVE-2026-35273 in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue since 12 June 2026 and marks it as known to be used in ransomware campaigns. Since then the FBI has said, on 6 October, that a breach of its own jobs portal resulted from a contractor that failed to apply a patch explicitly issued for the platform — which Reuters, citing unnamed sources, identified as Oracle PeopleSoft — and on 9 October it announced another arrest of a suspected ShinyHunters member, saying the group has breached more than 140 organisations. Oracle’s next quarterly Critical Patch Update is due on 20 October. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: many transit authorities and railroads run PeopleSoft for HR, payroll and finance, and a web shell on that tier puts employee records and whatever directory and database credentials the application holds within an attacker’s reach. It is an IT-side risk, not an OT one. - Google Threat Intelligence / Mandiant report; corroborated by BleepingComputer and The Hacker News; FBI statements as reported by The Hacker News, with the platform identification attributed to Reuters’ unnamed sources; CVSS v3.1 score per the published CVE record and KEV status per the CISA catalogue; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Mandiant report 25 Sep 2026; FBI statements 6 Oct and 9 Oct 2026; KEV-listed 12 Jun 2026

item.title: [Low] Nozomi’s summer OT telemetry ranks transportation second for alerts per customer, behind manufacturing
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Vendor OT/IoT telemetry; transportation ranked second
item.description: Nozomi Networks Labs published its June–August 2026 OT and IoT telemetry review on 12 October. Ranked by alerts per organisation, manufacturing came first, transportation second and energy, utilities and waste third, displacing government. Credential-related techniques made up roughly a third of detections. Among alerts Nozomi could attribute to an actor, Scattered Spider accounted for close to half, and Russia-linked or Russian-speaking actors together for more than a third. Siemens PLCs and Rockwell products were among the most-detected vulnerable products, and Nozomi says 58 percent of 2026 vulnerabilities rate High or Critical, up from 48 percent in 2025. Two cautions apply: alerts per organisation measures what Nozomi customers’ sensors flagged, not a count of attacks, and the actor names are telemetry attributions, not confirmed intrusions. The report does not break out rail. The reading for rail is our editorial assessment: transportation’s place in the ranking reflects a sector whose networks are increasingly instrumented and noisy, and the credential share supports putting identity controls ahead of exotic OT exploits. - Nozomi Networks Labs blog; figures are Nozomi’s customer telemetry; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 12 Oct 2026; data June–August 2026

item.title: [Info] Dragos sees old worms — Sality, Conficker, WannaCry — turning up more often in OT incident calls, and warns the wrong cleanup can hurt more than the infection
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Vendor incident-response observation and cleanup guidance
item.description: Dragos’s Lesley Carhart and Jan Hoff wrote on 15 October that requests for help with legacy commodity malware such as Sality, Gammima, WannaCry and Conficker have risen sharply in recent years, and that many OT networks Dragos is called into carry between 20 and 70 distinct commodity-malware variants across several subnets, often on systems older than Windows XP Service Pack 2. They attribute the rise to more networking and remote access, better visibility, and regulation that expects critical-infrastructure networks to be clean. Their answer is a “Now / Next / Never” framework, with a white paper, for deciding what to clean immediately, what to schedule and what to leave contained, and a warning that the wrong cleanup can be riskier than the infection itself. No actor or campaign is involved. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: signalling-support, SCADA and passenger-information estates are full of long-lived Windows hosts that suppliers certify and operators cannot simply rebuild, which is exactly the population Dragos describes. - Dragos blog; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 15 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] ENISA’s 2026 threat landscape puts transport among the most-targeted sectors and lists railway as highly critical but less mature
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — EU threat landscape report; railway named as high-criticality, lower-maturity
item.description: The EU Agency for Cybersecurity published its Threat Landscape 2026 on 22 September, covering events from 1 January to 31 December 2025. Cybercrime was the largest category at 36 percent of events, with ransomware 40 percent of those; hacktivists made 4,709 claims against EU member states, more than 89 percent of them DDoS; and more than 48,000 CVEs were published in 2025, up 22 percent. Public administration was the most targeted sector at 32 percent, followed by business services and transport at 8 percent each and manufacturing at 7 percent, and ENISA says 73 percent of targeted organisations were essential or important entities under NIS2. Citing its NIS360 assessment, ENISA lists railway — with health, maritime, ICT service management, space, public administration, and drinking and waste water — among sectors that are highly critical but less mature. The press release carries no OT-specific findings. The operational reading is our editorial assessment: for European infrastructure managers and railway undertakings this is the agency’s own view of where the sector stands, and the volume of hacktivist DDoS claims is a reminder that passenger-facing websites and apps are usually the first casualty. - ENISA Threat Landscape 2026 press release; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 22 Sep 2026; reporting period 2025

item.title: [Low] A security researcher found a rail operator’s production database exposed with live administrator sessions — routes, schedules and announcements were one step away
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Researcher-found exposure at an unnamed rail operator, IT/web, not exploited
item.description: Wiz published results of its “Scan for Good” programme on 24 September: an AI-assisted scan of public-facing systems at critical-infrastructure organisations, run with a supporting statement from CISA’s acting director. One finding concerns a public rail operator, which Wiz does not name or place in a country. In Wiz’s words, “a leaked production database exposed active administrator sessions, enabling control of routes, schedules, service announcements, and administrator accounts.” Wiz says it worked with the operator to secure the system before public transportation could be disrupted. Nothing in the report indicates that an attacker found or used the exposure, and no train-control, signalling or other OT system is described — this is the web and back-office layer. It is on this page because of what that layer controls. Passenger-information, scheduling and service-announcement platforms are rarely inside the TSA critical-cyber-system boundary, yet a hijacked administrator session there can publish false departures, cancel services on screen or push misleading announcements across stations — a disruption passengers experience as the railway itself failing. - Wiz research blog “Scan for Good” (verified 25 Sep 2026); also reported by Cybersecurity Dive; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Recorded Future expects Russia’s hybrid pressure on Europe to escalate over two years — logistics firms are flagged as high-risk, though no rail incident is cited
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Analytic assessment of Russia-linked hybrid activity in Europe; no rail incident cited
item.description: Recorded Future’s Insikt Group published an assessment on 24 September that Russia has escalated what Insikt calls “New Generation Warfare” (NGW) tactics in Europe since February 2022. It describes current activity as “largely opportunistic” rather than a coordinated campaign, but judges Russia “likely to escalate NGW tactics over the next two years, potentially culminating in a full-scale NGW campaign.” The incidents it cites include an explosive maritime drone intercepted near Romania’s Neptun Deep offshore gas field on 20 August, a sabotage plot using military-grade explosives against cargo infrastructure at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport in August, DDoS and access operations against the Norwegian public sector on 30 August, and Russian drones in Estonian airspace on 1 September. Its analyst adds that “outside of traditional critical infrastructure, logistics and dual-use firms are at high risk.” Recommendations include contractor and insider vetting, perimeter detection and counter-drone measures, law-enforcement partnerships, alternative supply routes, coordination with national CERTs and phishing-resistant MFA. The attribution is Insikt’s analytic assessment, and no specific unit is named. Nothing in it concerns a railway. It is here as context for European operators, and the rail relevance is our editorial assessment: the pattern it describes pairs physical interference with cyber and information operations, which is exactly the combination a rail incident process has to tell apart quickly. - Recorded Future Insikt Group blog; reported by Dark Reading; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] FDD warns that NATO reinforcement across Europe runs through civilian ports and railways with uneven cyber rules — and that Chinese-linked firms operate terminals in about half the EU ports NATO relies on
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Think-tank analysis of military-mobility corridors; no incident
item.description: The Foundation for Defense of Democracies published a report on 28 September by Jiwon Ma, a senior policy analyst at its Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation, titled Strengthening NATO Through Military Mobility and Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity. As reported by Industrial Cyber, it finds that three port groups — COSCO Shipping, China Merchants Group and Hutchison Port Holdings — own or operate terminals in roughly half of the EU ports considered critical to NATO operations; that firms FDD describes as Chinese state-linked hold stakes in more than 30 European port terminals, including facilities designated to receive US forces; and that they operate at no fewer than 14 of the 29 European ports near NATO naval facilities. For rail, the report’s point is scale and dependency: it notes that moving a single light division can take up to 200 trains, and that rail, unlike military air transport, has no mechanism for pooling assets, so it recommends jointly procuring or designating a minimum pool of dual-use heavy-lift wagons. Its cyber finding is that governance split across NATO, the EU and national authorities leaves the civilian transport operators that alliance forces depend on without consistent security standards. Other recommendations include aligning investment with reinforcement plans, annual national military-mobility annexes, organising NATO cyber-defence work around critical-infrastructure operators, tighter EU investment screening on military corridors, measures against satellite interference, and treating cyber workforce shortages as a defence priority. This is policy analysis from a think tank, not an incident or a government finding, and it names no compromised operator. The rail relevance for European infrastructure managers and freight operators on reinforcement corridors is our editorial assessment: a defence role can arrive without a matching security requirement, and the terminal at the port end of a rail movement may be run by a party whose systems you exchange data with but do not control. - Foundation for Defense of Democracies report by Jiwon Ma, as reported by Industrial Cyber; “Chinese state-linked” is FDD’s characterisation; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Report published 28 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Microsoft profiles Storm-2570, a ransomware affiliate that switches between Qilin, DragonForce, Anubis and BERT while its tradecraft stays the same — transportation is on its victim list
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Ransomware affiliate profile, transportation among victim sectors
item.description: Microsoft Threat Intelligence published a profile on 24 September of Storm-2570, a ransomware affiliate it has tracked since April 2025 that deploys Qilin, DragonForce, Anubis or BERT depending on the operation. Victims are in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Spain, the Netherlands and Puerto Rico, across sectors including transportation, energy, critical manufacturing, chemicals, healthcare, education, government and financial services. Microsoft says the group’s initial access “remains unconfirmed”. What stays consistent is what happens next: legitimate remote-management tools (Atera, MeshAgent, ScreenConnect, Splashtop and NinjaRMM), lateral movement with PsExec, Impacket and NetExec, credential theft with Mimikatz, LaZagne and ntdsutil, and exfiltration with Rclone and s5cmd. Microsoft names no victims and no rail operator is identified. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: the point of the profile is that the ransomware brand changes while the behaviour does not, so detection built on tooling and behaviour — unapproved remote-management agents, PsExec from unexpected hosts, bulk Rclone transfers — keeps working when the ransom note names a different gang. - Microsoft Security Blog (Microsoft Threat Intelligence); rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA publishes a cyber-decoys guide — detection you can add without touching a vital system
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Federal detection guidance
item.description: CISA released “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” on 17 September. It defines decoys as assets that appear to be legitimate systems, accounts or data but exist to distract adversaries, reveal their presence and support threat-intelligence collection, and it sets out three phases — preparation, execution and analysis — positioning the technique alongside Zero Trust rather than as a replacement for it. The reason this matters more in rail than in most sectors is what it does not require. Decoys, honeytokens and tripwire accounts are additive: a credential that should never be used, a fake engineering share, a dummy historian tag, a service account that exists only to be alerted on. None of that changes a signalling, interlocking or traction-power system, which is normally the reason detection work stalls on a railway — the asset owner will not accept a change to a vital system for a monitoring benefit. This is guidance, not a threat item: no vulnerability, no incident and no product is involved. - CISA guide “Using Cyber Decoys to Strengthen Detection and Response” — corroborated by SecurityWeek and Industrial Cyber - Published 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Two August counts, one direction: Comparitech logged a record 997 ransomware attacks and NCC Group 1,073, with industrial victims the largest share — and a newer group, Aurora, lists transportation among its targets
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Sector statistics
item.description: Comparitech data reported on 14 September recorded 997 ransomware attacks worldwide in August 2026 — about 32 a day, 23 percent more than July’s 809 and above the previous monthly record of 988 — with utility, healthcare and business-services attacks singled out as the categories behind the rise. NCC Group’s August review, reported by Industrial Cyber on 28 September, counts 1,073 attacks, up 12 percent from 960 in July, with the industrial sector the largest target at 329 attacks (31 percent), North America at 473 (44 percent) and Europe at 276 (26 percent); Qilin led with 164, overtaking The Gentlemen. NCC also profiles Aurora, a ransomware-as-a-service group active since late April 2026 whose targets include manufacturing, legal, research and development, and transportation: it gets in through VPN exploitation and credential harvesting, then encrypts hypervisors, taking every hosted virtual machine down at once. Both counts rest on leak-site claims and disclosure practice, which is why the totals differ; claimed victims are not confirmed victims, and neither tracker names a rail operator. For rail and transit the exposure is rarely the signalling system itself — it is dispatch support, crew management, maintenance planning, fare collection and passenger information, much of which now runs as virtual machines on a small number of hypervisors. - Comparitech monthly ransomware tracking and NCC Group’s August 2026 review, both via Industrial Cyber; counts are leak-site based - Data for August 2026; reporting 14 Sep 2026 and 28 Sep 2026

item.title: [Info] DOE and Idaho National Laboratory start a weekly Cyber-Informed Engineering series — rail’s fail-safe tradition is the same idea, applied on purpose
item.category: Threat Intelligence & Research — Federal engineering-practice series, voluntary
item.description: The Department of Energy’s Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response (CESER) and Idaho National Laboratory announced on 13 October a weekly “CIE Back-to-School” series that works through the twelve principles of Cyber-Informed Engineering one at a time, each with an overview, a case study and questions for engineers, starting with consequence-focused design. A new, simplified CIE Handbook is due at the end of the series. The argument behind CIE is that the security question belongs upstream, in design: identify the physical consequences that actually matter, then engineer them out with controls that do not depend on the digital system staying trustworthy. The series is aimed at energy infrastructure and is voluntary guidance, not regulation. The rail connection is our editorial assessment. Interlocking, fail-safe signalling and vital logic exist precisely so that an upstream failure cannot produce an unsafe movement; CIE asks that those principles be applied deliberately to newer digital systems rather than assumed to still hold. It is the most useful lens available for operators whose detection budget will never match their consequence exposure. - DOE CESER and Idaho National Laboratory announcement, as reported by Industrial Cyber; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Series announced 13 Oct 2026; reported 14 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Google’s threat intelligence group documents a credential campaign run end to end by autonomous agents in under six hours — and exploited vulnerabilities now arriving at about 18 a month
item.category: Threat Intel — Autonomous intrusion tooling and AI-era exploitation trends
item.description: Google’s Threat Intelligence Group reported on 8 September that a financially motivated group completed a large-scale credential-harvesting campaign in less than six hours using an autonomous multi-agent framework, with the agents rather than human operators carrying it through. GTIG separately observed actors stealing AI API credentials and running unauthorised workloads inside victims’ own cloud tenants across healthcare, government and media, and its guidance is to assume every actor is now using AI to some degree. On 30 September GTIG followed with data on vulnerability discovery and exploitation: monthly disclosures roughly doubled from 5,045 in January 2026 to 10,477 in July and reached 10,740 in August, while exploited vulnerabilities averaged 18 a month from January to August against 10.5 a month in 2025 — 141 distinct exploited flaws in eight months, against 127 in all of 2025. Edge and security appliances made up 14 percent of the exploited flaws, and more than 65 percent of those carried GTIG’s high or critical risk ratings; half of AI-discovered vulnerabilities were remote code execution, against 26 percent across the wider CVE ecosystem. GTIG does not discuss OT, industrial control systems or rail; that connection is ours. The rail consequence is arithmetic, not novelty. Credential phishing against dispatchers, crew callers, maintenance planners and contractor accounts is the standard opening move, and a campaign that completes inside six hours finishes well before a Monday-morning review — and comfortably inside the overnight window when the operations control centre is staffed but the security team is not. More exploited edge flaws each month also means the remote-access gear on this page’s advisory list will keep arriving faster than a slow patch cycle can absorb. - Google Threat Intelligence Group reporting of 8 Sep 2026, via The Hacker News; GTIG blog on vulnerability discovery and exploitation trends in the AI era; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 8 Sep 2026 and 30 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Ivanti Connect Secure: a three-bug chain gave attackers root on fully patched VPNs — one CVE is fixed and in KEV, the privilege-escalation link is not
item.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-access VPN, exploited chain, KEV-listed, one link unpatched
item.description: Ivanti disclosed on 13 October that CVE-2026-104935 in Connect Secure had been exploited against a limited number of customers. The CVE covers two flaws — an authentication bypass by spoofing and a file write — that together let a remote, unauthenticated attacker run commands; Ivanti rates it CVSS v3.1 8.6. Volexity, which found the activity during an incident response, says the attackers added a third bug, a privilege escalation that has no CVE and no patch yet, to reach root on an appliance that was fully patched at the time. Exploitation dates from at least early October: Volexity’s case begins on 3 October and Defused saw activity from 1 October. Volexity tracks the operator as UTA0576, a new actor. It left no web shell or backdoor and ran commands through the exploit requests themselves, then stole LDAP and domain credentials, queried Active Directory for LAPS passwords and BitLocker keys, Kerberoasted, sprayed passwords, sniffed LDAP traffic and wiped the appliance’s logs. Volexity has only low confidence that the motive is criminal rather than espionage. CISA added the CVE to KEV on 13 October with a 16 October deadline and, like Volexity, warns that Ivanti’s Integrity Checker Tool may not detect this compromise, because the chain patches code in memory and restores configuration. Fixed releases are 22.8R2.5, 25.1.1.2, 25.1.3.0 and 25.1.3.1; Ivanti says a fix for the third bug will follow in the coming weeks. No rail or transit victim has been named. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: Connect Secure is a common VPN for contractors and remote engineers, and this actor went straight for the directory credentials that unlock what sits behind it. - Ivanti advisory as reflected in the CVE record; Volexity research; CISA KEV catalogue (15 Oct 2026 release); reported by SecurityWeek, CyberScoop and Cybersecurity Dive (Defused data); rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Disclosed and KEV-listed 13 Oct 2026; federal deadline 16 Oct 2026; exploitation from 1–3 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] NetScaler: a fourth critical SAML flaw lands on top of three exploited zero-days — builds that fixed September’s bugs need upgrading again, and patching does not evict an intruder
item.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-access gateway, three exploited zero-days in KEV plus a fourth critical flaw
item.description: Citrix disclosed CVE-2026-107406 in bulletin CTX697191 on the evening of 8 October, and it was widely reported on 9 October: a memory overflow in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances configured as a SAML service provider or identity provider, which Citrix says may lead to remote code execution or denial of service. It is rated CVSS v4.0 9.5, there is no workaround, Citrix says it is not aware of exploitation, and it was not in KEV as of CISA’s 15 October catalogue. The catch is the builds many operators installed in the past three weeks: as reported from Citrix’s bulletin, 14.1-73.37 to 14.1-73.41 and 13.1-64.23 to 13.1-64.28 remain vulnerable when the appliance acts as a SAML identity provider, so those must be upgraded again, to 14.1-73.46 or 13.1-64.29 or later (FIPS and NDcPP builds are listed separately). In guidance reported on 12 October, CISA urged customers to patch, warned that attackers use the crash bug CVE-2026-88779 to force reboots so that code planted through CVE-2026-88771 runs, and released detection rules. That sits on top of the exploited trio already in KEV: CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, each CVSS v4 9.5 and listed on 27 September, and CVE-2026-88779, listed on 4 October, which Citrix and watchTowr describe as denial of service. Mandiant ties the campaign to suspected state-nexus actors, names no group and counts dozens of affected organisations in North America and Europe; Arctic Wolf’s figure of at least 78 counts targeted organisations, not confirmed victims; Shadowserver sees more than 20,000 exposed or potentially vulnerable appliances. Reported post-exploitation tooling includes custom PHP web shells, and Mandiant warns that upgrading alone does not remove access an intruder already has. No rail or transit victim has been named. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: NetScaler Gateway is a common front door for supplier and remote-engineer access, and on many railways and transit agencies it is the path by which signalling, SCADA and fare-system contractors reach the OT DMZ. - Citrix bulletins CTX697174 and CTX697191; CISA KEV catalogue (15 Oct 2026 release); CISA guidance, Mandiant, Arctic Wolf and Shadowserver figures via Cybersecurity Dive; SAML build details via The Hacker News and iTnews; watchTowr via SecurityWeek; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Exploited trio KEV-listed 27 Sep and 4 Oct 2026; CVE-2026-107406 disclosed 8 Oct 2026; CISA patch guidance reported 12 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] A suspected PRC-nexus actor exploited a BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day from late August — the kind of console suppliers use to reach plant PCs
item.category: Critical Advisory — Remote-support appliance, exploited zero-day, suspected state-nexus actor
item.description: BeyondTrust and Google Threat Intelligence Group disclosed on 15 October that CVE-2026-102764, a flaw in Remote Support’s internal messaging components that lets attackers perform file operations on the appliance, had been exploited as a zero-day since late August. BeyondTrust, as CVE numbering authority, scores it CVSS v4.0 9.3, and every Remote Support release up to 26.2.3 is affected. GTIG attributes the exploitation, and the follow-on SAWFLY web shell and BARECLAW tunneller, to the suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor it tracks as ARMORY CASTLE (formerly UNC5221), on the basis of tooling and tradecraft overlap. SecurityWeek reports two appliances compromised, one hosted by BeyondTrust and one self-hosted; the attackers gained root, harvested credentials, deleted logs and used the tool’s file transfer to pull documents from users’ desktops. BeyondTrust shipped a fix, patch BT26-05-RS, on 8 October and had patched its SaaS customers by 9 October; self-hosted appliances without automatic updates must be patched by hand, and releases older than 24.3.1 must be upgraded first. The CVE was not in KEV as of CISA’s 15 October catalogue. GTIG names no victims or sectors. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: remote-support consoles of this kind are how many signalling, SCADA and building-systems suppliers reach the engineering workstations they commissioned, and a console under someone else’s control reaches everything its sessions do. - Google Threat Intelligence Group report; BeyondTrust advisory BT26-05 as reflected in the CVE record and reported by SecurityWeek; CISA KEV catalogue (15 Oct 2026 release); rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Disclosed 15 Oct 2026; fix shipped 8 Oct 2026; exploitation from late Aug 2026

item.title: [Critical] Six more exploited flaws enter KEV in three days — PAN-OS management, Cisco’s email gateway, a Windows Mark-of-the-Web bypass, AhsayCBS backup and Atlassian Data Center
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed, firewall management, email gateway, Windows, backup and collaboration servers
item.description: Beyond Ivanti, CISA added six exploited flaws to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 13, 14 and 15 October, each with a three-day federal deadline. CVE-2026-96951, listed on 13 October, is the exploited zero-day in Microsoft’s October Patch Tuesday: a Windows Shell security-feature bypass that evades Mark of the Web, so downloaded files run without the usual warning; it needs user interaction and is scored CVSS v3.1 8.8. The release as a whole fixed more than 1,400 CVEs. CVE-2026-0322, listed on 14 October, lets an authenticated attacker with network access to the PAN-OS management interface run code as root on PA-Series, VM-Series and Panorama (CVSS v4.0 8.6 per Palo Alto); Palo Alto reports very limited exploitation and published attacker IP addresses. CVE-2026-76519, also 14 October and scored CVSS 9.8 by Cisco, lets an unauthenticated sender write files and run commands as root on Cisco Secure Email Gateway through a crafted attachment, where file reputation is enabled on a mail policy and Content Scanner Tools are older than 25.3.0.5525; it is the second exploited flaw in that product in a month. AhsayCBS CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134, listed the same day, chain an authentication flaw and a command injection in a backup server; Huntress saw them used to plant web shells and cryptocurrency miners, and Ahsay says its August patches were incomplete. CVE-2026-21589, listed on 15 October, lets an unauthenticated attacker read known files from the web root of Atlassian Data Center products including Confluence, Jira and Bitbucket. On 8 October CISA had also listed five much older flaws, in ISC BIND, Apache Struts, Strapi, ONLYOFFICE Docs and ProFTPD. No rail victim is named in any of these. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: PAN-OS often sits at the IT/OT boundary, Windows engineering workstations and HMIs are where a Mark-of-the-Web bypass lands, and the backup server is what a ransomware crew wants to own before it encrypts. - CISA KEV catalogue (15 Oct 2026 release); Palo Alto Networks and Cisco advisories; vendor details as reflected in the CVE records; Microsoft Patch Tuesday via SecurityWeek; AhsayCBS via The Hacker News (Huntress research); rail relevance is our editorial assessment - KEV additions 8, 13, 14 and 15 Oct 2026; federal deadlines 11–18 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] SonicWall SMA1000: a CVSS 10 pre-authentication flaw drew exploitation attempts within two days of the fix — not in KEV, and not a confirmed breach
item.category: Advisory — Secure-access gateway, CVSS 10, exploitation attempts, not KEV-listed
item.description: SonicWall published advisory SNWLID-2026-0017 on 6–7 October for CVE-2026-102255, a server-side request forgery in the WorkPlace interface of SMA1000 secure-access appliances (SMA 6210, 7210 and 8200v). Reached through an unintended alternate path, it lets an unauthenticated attacker make the appliance send requests to its own internal functions; CISA’s enrichment scores it CVSS v3.1 10.0, and SonicWall calls it maximum severity. The same release fixed three authenticated flaws: CVE-2026-102256, an administrator command injection; CVE-2026-102257, a Zip Slip in the management console; and CVE-2026-102258, a stored cross-site scripting bug. Defused saw its first hits on SMA1000 decoys on 8 October, and Previdian counted 135 attempts from two US addresses. Those are attempts against sensors: no source has established a successful breach of a customer network, and the CVE was not in KEV as of CISA’s 15 October catalogue. Fixed builds are 12.4.3-03670 and 12.5.0-03082 or later; there is no workaround, and SMA 100 and firewall SSL VPN are not affected. SMA1000 has been exploited repeatedly in 2026, so attempts this fast are not a surprise. No rail victim is named. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: SMA1000 is a secure-access gateway of the kind suppliers and remote staff use to reach operational support systems. - SonicWall advisory SNWLID-2026-0017 as reflected in the CVE record; CVSS per CISA enrichment; Defused and Previdian data via SecurityWeek and The Hacker News; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Advisory 6–7 Oct 2026; attempts from 8 Oct 2026; reported 12 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] October’s OT Patch Tuesday: Siemens S7-1500 web-server flaws at CVSS 9.6 with no fix yet, a Rockwell ArmorBlock takeover, and RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW fixes
item.category: Advisory — October OT vendor Patch Tuesday, no reported exploitation
item.description: Siemens published 17 new advisories on 13 October, by SecurityWeek’s count. The most serious, SSA-591731, covers eight web-server flaws in SIMATIC S7-1500, ET 200SP and ET 200pro CPUs and drive controllers, rated CVSS v3.1 9.6 by Siemens: an attacker can run code in an authorised user’s browser and perform PLC operations with that user’s rights. All versions are affected and only mitigations are available so far. SSA-832641 fixes authenticated path-traversal flaws in Industrial Edge devices (up to CVSS v3.1 9.1), with no fix yet for SCALANCE LPE9413 and LPE9433 or the affected HMI panels; SSA-784472 lists 377 CVEs in the optional Linux subsystem of the S7-1500 TM MFP technology module, also unfixed. SSA-508506 covers 11 flaws in RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW, including SQL injection and retrieval of administrator credentials, up to CVSS 8.8, fixed in V6.0. Rockwell’s only new advisory, SD1801, covers 1732E ArmorBlock I/O modules at 3.012 and earlier: CVE-2026-12655 (CVSS v3.1 9.1) lets an unauthenticated attacker change the web-server password and take over the module, and CVE-2026-12656 is a network-storm denial of service that needs a power cycle to clear; 3.013 fixes both. Schneider Electric issued SEVD-2026-286-02 for Sage RTUs that do not sufficiently verify firmware authenticity, fixed in C3414-500-S02L0, and SEVD-2026-286-01 for an unmaintained third-party component in Pro-face STW6000 and Harmony STW6 HMIs. None of these is reported exploited or listed in KEV. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: S7-1500 and ET 200SP controllers are common in depot, workshop, tunnel-ventilation and station plant; CROSSBOW is built to manage remote access to substation devices, a model traction-power estates also use; and RTUs of the Sage type can sit in traction-power and pumping SCADA. - Siemens ProductCERT SSA-591731, SSA-832641, SSA-784472 and SSA-508506; Rockwell Automation SD1801; Schneider Electric SEVD-2026-286-01 and -02; advisory count per SecurityWeek; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 13 Oct 2026; reported 14 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 6–15 October ICS advisories: an end-of-life building controller and a camera platform labelled for transportation, both unfixable, plus N-Tron switches and Ignition
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS releases 6–15 Oct, two transport-labelled items with no fix, no reported exploitation
item.description: CISA published ICS advisories on 6, 8, 13 and 15 October. Two list Transportation Systems among the sectors using the affected products, and neither has a fix. ICSA-26-279-01 republishes Johnson Controls’ JCI-PSA-2026-12 for EasyIO FG controller firmware: hard-coded credentials (CVE-2026-27872) and improper privilege management (CVE-2026-27873), each CVSS v3.1 7.7. The product is end-of-life, no fix will be issued, and Johnson Controls advises migrating to EasyIO Neo; CISA notes high attack complexity and that the flaws are not remotely exploitable. ICSA-26-288-02 covers Guangzhou Juan IoT’s EseeCloud app and firmware, used in low-cost IP cameras and recorders: hard-coded credentials at CVSS 9.8 (CVE-2026-107617) plus two medium flaws, and the vendor did not respond to CISA. Beyond the transport label, ICSA-26-281-01 covers seven flaws in Red Lion N-Tron 700 Series industrial Ethernet switches reported by Idaho National Laboratory, including factory administrator credentials that stay active, unauthenticated SNMP configuration changes and unsigned firmware updates (highest CVSS v3.1 8.3; the authentication bypass needs physical access); firmware 3.11.1 fixes them, and CISA updated the scores on 15 October. ICSA-26-286-01 covers a privilege-escalation flaw in Inductive Automation’s Ignition SCADA platform (CVE-2026-92817, CVSS v3.1 8.8), fixed in 8.1.55 and 8.3.9, and ICSA-26-288-01 six flaws in the open-source Eclipse Milo OPC UA library, fixed in 1.1.5 with no fix for the 0.6.x line. For energy, ICSA-26-279-06 covers Hitachi Energy’s end-of-life RTU500 CMU firmware, where CVE-2026-8065 (CVSS v3.1 9.1) allows unauthenticated firmware upload; the remedy is moving to supported firmware 12.7.8 or 13.9.1. CISA reports no known exploitation for any of them, and none is in KEV. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: EasyIO-class controllers run station heating, ventilation and lighting; low-cost camera platforms turn up at depots and car parks; N-Tron switches carry plant-room networks; Ignition is a common SCADA and HMI layer for station and facility systems; and RTU500 units can sit in traction-power substations. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-279-01, -279-06, -281-01, -286-01, -288-01 and -288-02, read via CISA’s CSAF data as mirrored by CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; CISA bulletin of 8 Oct 2026; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 6, 8, 13 and 15 Oct 2026; N-Tron advisory updated 15 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager and Fortinet FortiMail join KEV as exploited zero-days — one configures the routers at every station and depot, the other screens mail into the corporate side
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed, SD-WAN control plane and mail gateway
item.description: Cisco published an advisory on 30 September for CVE-2026-76504 in Catalyst SD-WAN Manager: improper handling of URI encoding lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker get past an authentication rule meant to protect an API endpoint and reach administrative-level access. Cisco scores it CVSS 9.8, offers no workaround, and says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in September; CISA added it to KEV the same day with a 3 October deadline, and Cisco revised the advisory on 2 October. Fixed releases are 20.9.10.1, 20.12.8.2, 20.15.6.1, 20.18.4.1, 26.1.2.1 and 26.2.1, and releases older than 20.9 must migrate to a fixed one. On 1 October Fortinet disclosed CVE-2026-104286 in FortiMail (FG-IR-26-175), a path-traversal and NULL-byte handling flaw that lets an unauthenticated attacker write arbitrary files on the appliance through crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests. Fortinet scores it CVSS 9.8 and says it has been reported exploited in the wild; CISA added it to KEV on 1 October with a 4 October deadline. Affected are FortiMail 7.2.0 to 7.2.9, 7.4.0 to 7.4.8, 7.6.0 to 7.6.6 and 8.0.0 to 8.0.1; Fortinet’s 5 October update lists fixed releases 7.4.9, 7.6.7 and 8.0.2, and tells 7.2 customers to move to 7.4 or later. Neither vendor has named an actor or victims, and nothing ties either flaw to rail. The rail fit is our editorial assessment: SD-WAN Manager is the controller that pushes configuration and policy to the edge routers in stations, depots, yards and wayside communication huts, so administrative access there is a route to rewriting segmentation at every site at once; FortiMail sits on the corporate side, where a compromised mail gateway can read, alter or send the messages that open most intrusions against dispatch and operations staff. - Cisco advisory cisco-sa-sdwan-webauth-xr8beuuU (revised 2 Oct 2026); Fortinet PSIRT FG-IR-26-175; CISA KEV catalogue; reported by BleepingComputer and SecurityWeek; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Cisco advisory and KEV listing 30 Sep 2026; FortiMail disclosure and KEV listing 1 Oct 2026; Fortinet fixed-release update 5 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] MikroTik: the exploited “MikroTrick” SSH chain is in KEV with every deadline passed, and CISA adds a CVSS 9.8 pre-authentication web-management flaw that is not — the router class that quietly backhauls remote rail sites
item.category: Critical Advisory — Edge routers, chain confirmed exploited and KEV-listed; new pre-authentication flaw not in KEV
item.description: CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue holds three MikroTik RouterOS flaws: CVE-2026-86060, an argument-injection flaw, and CVE-2026-67277, a missing-authentication flaw in the bandwidth-test service, both added on 10 September; and CVE-2026-67279, an SSH flaw added on 25 September that lets an unauthenticated client open a session channel and send an exec request and, in KEV’s words, “can be chained to achieve unauthenticated exploitation of CVE-2026-86060”. The federal deadlines of 13 and 28 September have both passed. CERT Polska reported on 5 September that this SSH chain, which it calls MikroTrick, had been exploited in the wild since about 2 September, before patches existed, and its 22 September analysis confirms that CVE-2026-67279 combined with CVE-2026-86060 gives an unauthenticated attacker full administrative control. CVE-2026-67276, which some earlier coverage placed in the chain, is not in KEV. Fixed builds for the chain are RouterOS 7.24.2, 7.23.4 and 6.49.21, plus 7.25beta3; a related flaw, CVE-2026-67278, needs 7.24.3 or 7.23.6 because the earlier fix was incomplete. On 29 September CISA published advisory ICSA-26-272-06 for a separate flaw, CVE-2026-84411: an integer underflow in RouterOS’s HTTP request-body handling, reachable before authentication, that can give remote code execution as root, or a denial of service, from a single crafted request. It is scored CVSS v3.1 9.8 and v4 9.3, affects versions before 7.24 and is fixed from 7.24; CISA reports no known public exploitation, and it is not in KEV. Read literally, CISA’s affected range takes in the 7.23 and 6.49 builds that fix the SSH chain, so check MikroTik’s release notes before treating a device on those lines as covered. No victims, sectors or actor have been named for any of these flaws, and nothing ties the activity to rail. The relevance for this audience is our editorial assessment: low-cost RouterOS hardware, including its cellular models, is a common choice for backhaul and telemetry at remote, unstaffed sites such as crossings, wayside cabinets, yard offices and small stations, and a router compromised at that layer sits upstream of whatever segmentation you rely on. - CERT Polska advisories and its 22 Sep technical analysis; CISA KEV catalogue; CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-272-06 (CVE-2026-84411); The Hacker News on CVE-2026-67279; no victim, sector or actor named in any source; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - CERT Polska 5 Sep 2026; KEV additions 10 Sep and 25 Sep 2026; CISA advisory ICSA-26-272-06 29 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 29 September and 1 October ICS batches lean on transport: a Lantronix cellular gateway whose firmware checks can be defeated, IP cameras at CVSS 10.0 with public exploit code, and an EV-charging platform with no version fix
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS batches, transport-labelled devices, no reported exploitation
item.description: CISA published seven ICS advisories on 29 September (ICSA-26-272-01 to -07) and six on 1 October (ICSA-26-274-01 to -06), and more than half of them list Transportation Systems among the sectors using the affected products. The one closest to rail infrastructure is ICSA-26-272-01, for the Lantronix G520 Series cellular gateway: firmware 2.6.0.4R6_stable carries an improper verification of cryptographic signature flaw (CVE-2026-91191) and a cross-site scripting flaw (CVE-2026-84409), each CVSS v3.1 7.5 and v4 7.7, which CISA says could allow an attacker to replace software and execute arbitrary code with root privileges. Version 2.6.0.7R6 fixes both, and CISA names Transportation Systems, Energy, and Water and Wastewater as the sectors. ICSA-26-272-03 covers command injection in VIVOTEK camera firmware across 37 models (CVE-2026-22755, CVSS v3.1 10.0 and v4 9.3), for which public proof-of-concept code exists; the fix is current firmware. ICSA-26-274-02 covers every version of Monta’s monta.app EV-charging platform, where missing authentication on a WebSocket interface allows charging-station impersonation (CVE-2026-95102, CVSS v3.1 9.4 and v4 9.3); there is no fixed version, only Monta’s guidance to enable OCPP 1.6 Security Profile 2 and its statement that rate limiting is in place. ICSA-26-274-01 covers Armatura One physical access control below 4.7.2 (USA builds below 4.6.1), which embeds an ActiveMQ component carrying CVE-2023-46604 — a flaw already in KEV from attacks on other ActiveMQ deployments, though none is reported against Armatura — plus hard-coded keys and credentials; 4.7.2 and 4.6.1_USA fix it. The other transport-labelled items are the Viidure dashcam Android app, with hard-coded cloud credentials (CVSS 10.0) and no fix planned; two lower-scored, fixed Johnson Controls EasyIO Neo controller flaws; and Toptech TMS7 and TopHAT terminal-management software, with a CVSS 10.0 flaw fixed in 7.8. CISA reports no known exploitation for any advisory in either batch. The MikroTik advisory in the 29 September batch is covered in its own card. The rail relevance is our editorial assessment: cellular gateways of the G520 type backhaul crossings, wayside cabinets, substations and vehicle telemetry; IP cameras and access control sit in every station; and transit agencies electrifying bus fleets run depot charging platforms of exactly the Monta type. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-272-01 to -07 and ICSA-26-274-01 to -06, details checked against CISA’s CSAF data as ingested by CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 29 Sep 2026 and 1 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] Cisco Talos tracks three clusters exploiting Secure Firewall Management Center flaws CVE-2026-20079 and CVE-2026-20316 — that box is the IT/OT boundary TSA asks you to prove
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed, firewall management plane
item.description: Cisco and CISA confirmed on 9 September that CVE-2026-20079 in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center is under active exploitation. The flaw is a critical authentication bypass caused by an improper system process created at boot; a remote, unauthenticated attacker sends crafted HTTP requests and gains root on the appliance operating system. Cisco fixed it in early March and published indicators of compromise in late July, then disclosed on 9 September that it had observed exploitation from August. CISA added the CVE to KEV with a 12 September federal deadline, which has now passed. Cisco Talos tracks three clusters (its post was last revised on 21 September and still names the same three) of post-compromise activity across this flaw and the earlier CVE-2026-20316: UAT-12197, which used CVE-2026-20079 to plant a web shell and a JAR-based command executor and steal credentials; UAT-11823, an APT that used both flaws and deployed a Cyclops Blink variant (Talos notes a tooling overlap with a previously known actor but makes no attribution); and UAT-11988, which Talos assesses with high confidence to be a ransomware operator, and whose access Talos ties to CVE-2026-20316 (static credentials), not to CVE-2026-20079. CVE-2026-20316 is not in the KEV catalogue. On 16 September Cisco shipped its September hardening release for ASA, FTD and FMC (CVE-2026-20329 to CVE-2026-20336, maximum CVSS 9.9), and revised the FMC advisory to replace the earlier hot fixes with those security-hardening builds (7.0.10, 7.2.12, 7.4.8, 7.6.6, 7.7.13, 10.0.2 and 10.1.0); there is no workaround. Talos’s post was last revised on 21 September, and nothing rail-specific has been reported. For railroads and transit agencies the consequence is specific. TSA security directives require a documented, tested separation between IT and critical cyber systems — dispatch, signalling support, traction-power SCADA, fare and station systems. FMC is where that separation is enforced, and root there lets an attacker edit it silently. - Cisco security advisory update and Cisco Talos research of 9 Sep 2026, plus the CISA KEV addition of 9 Sep 2026 — reported by SecurityWeek; Talos cluster wording re-checked against the Talos post (revised 21 Sep 2026) on 22 Sep 2026 - Advisory updated and KEV listing added 9 Sep 2026; reporting 10 Sep 2026; hardening release published 16 Sep 2026; KEV status re-checked 22 Sep 2026; no new development found as of 27 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] Four more boundary products went into KEV on 22 September — Check Point VPN and management, Arista’s SD-WAN orchestrator and F5 APM, and the 25 September deadline has passed
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed, network edge and management plane
item.description: CISA added four actively exploited flaws to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 22 September, each with a federal remediation deadline of 25 September. Two are Check Point’s, confirmed in Check Point’s own advisories; neither Check Point nor the reporting gives a CVSS score, and we do not supply one. CVE-2026-85102 is improper certificate validation on Security Gateways and Spark firewalls running Site-to-Site or Remote Access VPN, giving unauthenticated remote code execution; patches shipped on 9 September and exploitation has been observed from 12 September. CVE-2026-93616 is a separate, pre-authentication path traversal affecting Security Management and Multi-Domain servers, log servers and SmartEvent that lets an attacker upload and execute scripts; Check Point says it was exploited as a zero-day in a handful of pinpointed attacks on 23 July. The third is Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator, CVE-2026-93952 (CVSS v3.1 10.0, v4.0 9.5), an input-validation flaw in on-premises orchestrators that Arista says is actively exploited; exposure requires certificate-based Edge-to-Orchestrator authentication, and hosted orchestrators are already patched. The fourth is F5 BIG-IP APM, CVE-2026-94127 (CVSS v3.1 9.8, v4.0 9.3), an unauthenticated heap overflow reachable only where a virtual server combines an APM access policy with an OAuth profile, fixed by engineering hotfixes; CISA and F5 advise applying F5’s iRule first, to allow forensic triage, and then the hotfix. No victim in any sector has been named and nothing ties these to rail. The rail fit is architectural: SD-WAN orchestrators push configuration to the edges in stations, depots and wayside communication huts; Check Point gateways often terminate supplier remote access; and the management server holds the policy that enforces the IT/OT separation TSA asks you to document. - CISA KEV alert of 22 Sep 2026; Check Point security advisory (22 Sep 2026); Arista Security Advisory 0183; F5 K000162605 as summarised by Rapid7; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Added to KEV 22 Sep 2026; federal remediation deadline 25 Sep 2026, now passed; no new development found as of 27 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Two critical lwIP flaws in two weeks — the MQTT client on 22 September, the SMTP client on 6 October — and the question is still which field devices ship them
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS advisories, embedded TCP/IP stack, no reported exploitation
item.description: CISA has now published two critical advisories for lwIP, the lightweight open-source TCP/IP stack built into a very wide range of embedded controllers, gateways, I/O modules and sensors. On 6 October ICSA-26-279-02 covered a classic buffer overflow in the SMTP client application of lwIP 2.2.1 (CVE-2026-15340, CVSS v3.1 9.8 per the advisory and v4.0 9.3 per the CVE record); the fix is an upstream patch and commit rather than a new release, and CISA names energy and water as the sectors. It follows ICSA-26-265-01 on 22 September, an out-of-bounds write in lwIP’s MQTT client (CVE-2026-87121, CVSS 9.8 v3.1 and 9.3 v4.0, network-reachable with no authentication or user interaction) that may give an attacker full code execution on the device; it was reported by Shahriyar Jalayeri of ByteRay. A separate double-free advisory published the same day, ICSA-26-265-02, was reported by Eric Evenchick of Tetrel Security; we could not verify its CVE or score, so none is quoted. Because lwIP is a library, exposure depends on whether a device maker compiled in the affected client application, and no downstream vendor list has been published for either flaw. The 22 September batch also carried two Siemens advisories that touch station estates: an unrestricted file upload in Siveillance Control, Siemens’ physical-security management platform, and a code-injection flaw in the Desigo CC building-management family, reported by Michelin CERT. No exploitation is reported for any of these. For rail, the plausible lwIP carriers are the telemetry gateways, condition-monitoring sensors and small controllers in traction-power, tunnel-ventilation and wayside cabinets, many of which publish over MQTT or send alarm email. - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-279-02 as mirrored by CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup; ICSA-26-265-01 and -02 and the 22 Sep 2026 batch as listed by Chemical Facility Security News; CVSS for CVE-2026-87121 per the published CVE record (Ubuntu CVE tracker); rail-device relevance is our editorial assessment - Published 22 Sep 2026 and 6 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] CISA adds a Zyxel GS1900 switch flaw to KEV after GreyNoise counts 996 compromised units — the kind of switch found in a station office, not a signal room
item.category: Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed, small-office switch
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-7273 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 21 September with a federal remediation deadline of 24 September. It is a stack-based buffer overflow in the CGI program of Zyxel GS1900-series managed switches (GS1900-8, 8HP, 10HP, 16, 24, 24E, 24EP, 24HPv2, 48 and 48HPv2) that lets an unauthenticated attacker with access to the management interface execute operating-system commands through a crafted HTTP request. Zyxel published the fix in June; its advisory gives no CVSS score and we do not supply one. On 21 September GreyNoise published what it describes as the first documented in-the-wild exploitation: a single actor, assessed by GreyNoise as Chinese-speaking, has compromised 996 GS1900 switches across 48 countries since about mid-August, including 129 in the United States and 66 in the Netherlands, using an obfuscated Python tool that pulled device configurations and root-level password hashes over TFTP; 564 of the victims were still on factory-default credentials. GreyNoise links the same actor to data theft from an unnamed western government organisation through two WordPress flaws, and describes it as related to, or the same as, the actor behind earlier Gitea exploitation — an inference, not an observation. No rail or transit victim is identified. Our assessment of the rail relevance: GS1900 is a small-office switch, and the place it turns up on a railway or transit property is the station back office, the yard office, the small agency’s headquarters LAN or a contractor’s site cabin, not the signalling or traction-power network. A compromised switch there yields a network foothold and every credential configured on it. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue (21 Sep 2026 update), GreyNoise research of 21 Sep 2026 and Zyxel’s June 2026 advisory; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Added to KEV 21 Sep 2026; GreyNoise report 21 Sep 2026; Zyxel fix published Jun 2026

item.title: [High] Three exploited Linux kernel flaws land in KEV with a three-day federal deadline — the question for rail is which appliances run Linux underneath
item.category: Advisory — Three additions to the CISA KEV catalogue
item.description: CISA added three Linux kernel vulnerabilities to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 18 September, across two alerts, with a federal remediation deadline of 21 September, which has now passed; no further exploitation detail has been published since the listing. CVE-2025-39682 is in the kernel TLS receive path, where a zero-length record can bypass record-type handling. CVE-2026-53266 is an out-of-bounds write in the netfilter bridge ebtables SNAT target, which can lead to memory corruption, denial of service or local privilege escalation on hosts with bridge netfilter rules configured. CVE-2025-39964 is a race condition in the AF_ALG crypto socket interface, exploitable by a local, low-privileged user. Published severity scores for the three differ widely between sources, so none is quoted here. CISA lists them as exploited in the wild, but no public detail says who is exploiting them or against what, and none is tied to a rail or OT target. None is a rail product. As with the Linux kernel addition of 27 August, the relevance is that traffic-management servers, passenger information systems, CCTV recorders and many wayside and on-board gateways run Linux underneath, often as vendor appliances patched on the supplier’s schedule. These are local, post-access bugs that let an attacker who already has a foothold go further, not ways in from the internet. - CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue (18 Sep 2026 update) and CISA alerts of 18 Sep 2026, with reporting by The Hacker News; rail relevance is our editorial assessment - Added to KEV 18 Sep 2026; federal remediation deadline 21 Sep 2026, passed; status re-checked 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Critical] A CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass in Cisco Identity Services Engine is being exploited — that is the box deciding who gets onto which network
item.category: Critical Advisory — Actively exploited, KEV-listed
item.description: Cisco published advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 on 16 September for CVE-2026-76460, a CVSS 10.0 flaw in Identity Services Engine and ISE-PIC. An API endpoint with insufficient authentication lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker bypass the web-based management interface, and Cisco states that its PSIRT is aware of active exploitation. All versions are affected; fixes are 3.1 Patch 12, 3.2 Patch 11, 3.3 Patch 12, 3.4 Patch 7 and 3.5 Patch 4. There are no workarounds — restricting management traffic with infrastructure access control lists is the only mitigation Cisco offers. CISA added the CVE to the KEV catalogue on 16 September with a three-day federal deadline of 19 September, which has now passed. No actor attribution has been published, and no critical-infrastructure or OT targeting has been claimed; Singapore’s Cyber Security Agency reinforced the advisory with its own alert on 21 September. ISE 3.0 is end-of-life and gets no fix, so those deployments must migrate. The rail relevance is structural rather than reported: ISE is the network access control and policy engine many railroads and transit authorities use to decide which port, VLAN and remote session a device or contractor is allowed, including the segmentation between corporate systems and dispatch, signalling support, traction-power SCADA and station estates. Root over the policy engine is root over the boundary. Separately, CISA added Cisco Secure Email Gateway CVE-2026-76461 to KEV on 14 September, due 17 September — a second exploited Cisco entry point in the same week. - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-ISE-ABP-VNSW7Tn5 and the CISA KEV catalogue — corroborated by SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer - Advisory published and KEV listing added 16 Sep 2026; federal deadline 19 Sep 2026 passed; status re-checked 22 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Moxa fixes an unauthenticated crash in the web login of its TN-4500B switches — a line it markets for rolling-stock networks
item.category: Advisory — On-board train Ethernet switch, availability only
item.description: Moxa published security advisory MPSA-252620 on 18 September for CVE-2026-15579 in its TN-4500B Ethernet switch series, a line Moxa markets for rolling-stock networks: its product page describes the ToughNet TN-4500B switches as designed for railway applications including rolling stock, and as meeting the EN 50155 test requirements. The flaw is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) in the web login: the username field is not length-checked, so a remote, unauthenticated attacker who can reach the web interface can send an overlong value and crash the authentication process. The impact Moxa describes is denial of service, with no confidentiality loss; it scores the flaw CVSS v4 8.8 (vector AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:H) and rates it High. Firmware v2.0 and earlier is affected and v2.1 or later fixes it. The advisory makes no statement about exploitation, and we found no report of attacks. Our assessment of the rail relevance: switches of this class usually sit inside the train, carrying the on-board network, so the reachable question is which vehicle networks and train-to-ground links expose the switch’s web management at all. - Moxa security advisory MPSA-252620 (CVE-2026-15579, credited to Mask Lu); product description from Moxa’s TN-4500B Series page; rail-network relevance is our editorial assessment - Advisory published 18 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Twenty flaws in Pepperl+Fuchs IO-Link masters, two of them CVSS 9.8 and unauthenticated — the same CVE set appears under Phoenix Contact and Carlo Gavazzi badges, and Nozomi has now published the attack chain
item.category: Advisory — Vendor firmware fix, CVSS 9.8, no reported exploitation
item.description: CERT@VDE published VDE-2026-014 on 16 September for 20 vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-27546 to CVE-2026-27565) in the firmware of Pepperl+Fuchs ICE2-8IOL and ICE3-8IOL IO-Link master modules, found by Nozomi Networks researchers. Firmware below 1.7.4 is affected and 1.7.8 fixes them. The two worst are CVE-2026-27546, an authentication bypass, and CVE-2026-27565, an unauthenticated upload of a malicious IODD device-description file that executes shell scripts, both CVSS v3.1 9.8. The remainder (CVE-2026-27547 to -27564) are command-injection, file-inclusion and authorisation flaws between 7.2 and 8.8 that lead to root-level code execution; CVE-2026-27557 (7.5) is an unauthenticated path traversal that reads the SSH server’s private keys, and CVE-2026-27553 (6.5) discloses password hashes. With the same CVE set, Phoenix Contact IOL MA8 PN DI8 and IOL MA8 EIP DI8 modules (VDE-2026-027, 20 CVEs) and Carlo Gavazzi YL212 and YN115 masters (VDE-2026-028) carry the same fixes on the same date. On 24 September Nozomi Networks Labs published its technical write-up of the Pepperl+Fuchs findings, tested on an ICE2-8IOL-K45P-RJ45 running EtherNet/IP firmware 1.7.3: it counts 19 CVEs on that module and shows that, chained, they give an unauthenticated attacker root on the device and the ability to manipulate sensor and actuator data. No exploitation is reported, and no CISA ICS advisory had covered the flaws through CISA’s 1 October batch. The rail relevance is our assessment rather than anything in the advisory: IO-Link masters sit at the sensor and actuator layer of discrete automation, which on a railway means depot and workshop equipment, wheel lathes, wash plants, material-handling and platform plant supplied by integrators, usually on PROFINET or EtherNet/IP segments the operator’s IT team has never inventoried. Nothing here touches signalling or train control. - CERT@VDE advisory VDE-2026-014 (Pepperl+Fuchs), with VDE-2026-027 (Phoenix Contact) and VDE-2026-028 (Carlo Gavazzi); Nozomi Networks Labs technical write-up; rail-estate relevance is our editorial assessment - CERT@VDE advisories 16 Sep 2026; Nozomi write-up 24 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Seven new ICS advisories and one update on 17 September — one of them a transport device, none of them exploited
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS batch, no reported exploitation
item.description: CISA published seven new advisories, ICSA-26-260-01 through -07, plus one update, on Thursday 17 September; the next batch followed on 22 September and is carried as a separate card. The advisory carrying CISA’s Transportation Systems label is ICSA-26-260-01, covering Bransys ELD for Android below 11.00.00 and for iOS below 1.1.54: hard-coded MQTT credentials (CVE-2026-86520, CVSS 7.5), cleartext transmission of sensitive information (CVE-2026-86689, 5.9) and hard-coded FTP credentials (CVE-2026-77960, 5.3), all fixed in the versions named. These are electronic logging devices for commercial road vehicles, so for a railroad or transit authority the exposure sits with fleet, maintenance-of-way and non-revenue vehicle telematics rather than anywhere near train control — it should not be read as a rail advisory. The most significant score in the batch is ICSA-26-260-02, a Mitsubishi Electric authentication-algorithm flaw in GX Works3 and Motion Control Settings affecting all versions (CVE-2026-15688, CVSS 8.8 v3.1 and 8.7 v4.0), which allows a local authentication bypass and tampering with control programs — relevant to workshop, depot and maintenance-facility automation. The remaining five cover Hitachi Energy FACTS Control Platform (-03, whose score we could not verify, so none is quoted), Schneider Electric Modicon M340 and X80 Ethernet communication modules (-04, CVE-2025-6625, a denial of service through a crafted FTP command, CVSS 7.5 v3.1 and 8.7 v4, fixed in M340 firmware SV3.70; a republication of Schneider’s 2025 advisory), Schneider Electric NetBotz 5 750 and 755 (-05, CVE-2026-13336 command injection at 6.4 v3.1 and 7.3 v4, plus CVE-2026-13337, fixed in 5.6.0), ABB Ability Edgenius (-06, the “Copy Fail” Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-31431 at 7.8, fixed in 3.2.4.1) and Schneider Electric PowerChute Serial Shutdown (-07, CVE-2026-13348, excessive authentication attempts, 5.3 v3.1 and 6.9 v4; see the vendor advisory for the fixed version). CISA also updated ICSA-26-211-07 (Mitsubishi CC-Link IE TSN) on 17 September to add eight affected products. No exploitation is reported for anything in the batch. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-260-01 to -07 and the update to ICSA-26-211-07 — scores for -01 and -04 to -07 checked against CISA’s CSAF files 20 Sep 2026 and re-checked 22 Sep 2026; -03 unscored and deliberately not quoted - Published 17 Sep 2026

item.title: [Medium] Rockwell extends its lockout-recovery guidance to Micro820 and Micro850, and MITRE now catalogues the PLC-tampering campaign behind it as C0066
item.category: Advisory — Vendor hardening and recovery guidance, revised
item.description: Rockwell Automation published revision 5.0 of security notice SD1790 on 18 September, its fifth revision since the notice first appeared on 30 July. The notice exists because of an FBI public service announcement of 30 July describing attackers who remotely altered the configuration of internet-exposed programmable logic controllers, changed IP addresses and set passwords where none had existed, locking the operators out. The original guidance covered MicroLogix 1100 and 1400; revision 5.0 extends the hardening and password-recovery instructions to the Micro820 and Micro850 controllers as well. There is no CVE: the notice is about exposure and configuration, not a software flaw. The controls Rockwell lists are the familiar ones — remove the controller from any internet-reachable path, put access behind a VPN and firewall, set strong passwords, keep offline backups of the project so a locked controller can be restored, disable the built-in HTTP server and keep firmware current. The revision adds no new incident data. MITRE has since documented the July 2026 intrusions behind that PSA as campaign C0066 in ATT&CK v20 (page created 8 October, updated 13 October): more than 30 Minnesota municipal water and wastewater utilities whose internet-facing MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 controllers had IP addresses and passwords changed, with program logic altered at one or more victims; MITRE says the campaign has not been formally attributed. Our assessment of the rail relevance: MicroLogix and Micro800-class controllers are the low-cost PLCs that end up in small, distributed installations built by contractors — pump and drainage stations, tunnel and station plant, yard equipment, small traction-power auxiliaries — often with a cellular modem for remote support and no entry in the operator’s OT asset register. The FBI describes a class of attack that needs no exploit at all, just reachability. - Rockwell Automation security notice SD1790 revision 5.0, referencing the FBI public service announcement of 30 Jul 2026; MITRE ATT&CK campaign C0066; rail installation pattern is our editorial assessment - Revision 5.0 published 18 Sep 2026; original notice 30 Jul 2026; MITRE C0066 created 8 Oct and updated 13 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Nozomi’s SCALANCE LPE9403 research now runs to twelve flaws, several chainable to root on an OT edge device — vendor-patched and unexploited
item.category: Advisory — Vendor patch, vulnerability research
